title: Notes of Ministry - 37 - December 1975

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 37 - December 1 (2413)/Notes of Ministry - 37 - Decemb - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I desire to speak simply of man’s relations with God. I therefore read about the Lord Jesus, because His relations with His God were perfect. He was absolutely perfect as Man. We have already referred to Him as without spot and without blemish; how everything within was perfect as well as without. We speak with the greatest reverence of Him, but every movement of His heart, every impulse and motive was perfectly in accord with His Father. It is a great thing to contemplate the perfect manhood of Jesus and to contemplate the delight the Father had in Him. His actions were pleasing to His Father, but those actions flowed from what was within, and the Father took account of that. I believe that is the reason that the Father says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have found my delight”. The Father took account of all His inward motives and every thought of His heart, and found His pleasure in Him. I suppose it refers to the thirty years of His life which very largely are hidden from us. But nothing in that perfect life was hidden from the Father and this is an expression of His pleasure when He says, “in whom I have found my delight”.

God had never had a man like this before. There were many types, and men of moral worth, but none before like Jesus, perfect in blood and flesh. That is probably the reason that when God arranges the centre of His tabernacle system it is not a man but it is the ark. No one could look into the ark, but we know from the Scriptures that it was the same within as it was without. It reminds one of the simple expression of Jesus, “Altogether that which I also say to you”, John 8: 25. His speech was the practical expression of what He was. Let us, therefore, contemplate Jesus as Man. One who, indeed, died for us and has been raised again and who, as from the right hand of God, sent out the Spirit so that we might be maintained in His character here. We can only be maintained in His character by His Spirit.

Now in the second scripture God is spoken to as the “knower of the hearts of all”. What a wonderful expression that is! There is no heart that is not known by Him. It says, “All things are naked and laid bare to his eyes, with whom we have to do” (Hebrews 4: 13), and He has to do with us, not looking at the outward appearance, however proper it may appear to be, but knowing every heart and, as knowing every heart, acting according to His sovereign will and knowledge. In the passage that we are considering both would appear to have been qualified for the office, but how wonderful that the “knower of the hearts of all” showed what His sovereign will was.

We must bow to this, dear brethren, that God Himself knows every heart and moves according to His own sovereign will. Hence He raises up persons to serve us. How much respect we have for those who have served us in the past. Our wisdom is to bow simply to His sovereignty, and make room for the ministry He has given through vessels He has chosen. There is no question that Judas had a commission. Somebody served with him when they were sent out two and two, but subsequently he was shamefully exposed and shown to have no affection for Christ. It is said, he went “to his own place”. All the crises, dear brethren, in the testimony expose where we really are with God. Whether for good or for evil, I believe each finds his own place morally. This is a sobering consideration.

I am not suggesting that any believer is Judas, but he is an extreme example of a person who in a crisis failed and went to his own place. All of us sitting here are known by God. How wonderful that in His presence we can judge ourselves, and be in simple liberty and communion with Him.

Now David is a wonderful example of the anointing. The anointing was upon him, but unquestionably it was upon a man who was according to God’s own heart. “I have found David, the son of Jesse, a man after my heart”, Acts 13: 22. That is inward, dear brethren. He too was under the eye of the Knower of all hearts, and God found in him a man after His own heart who, God says, “shall do all my will”. He is therefore a type of Jesus. David failed; he had to be searched and he invites the searching of God. Nevertheless, by the Holy Spirit he rises to be a wonderful type of Jesus.

Now these men of stature came before Samuel. Even a spiritual man like Samuel can be deceived. It is natural to us all to look on the outward appearance, but the word is, “Look not on his countenance … Jehovah looketh upon the heart”. As each person passes by he is rejected, pointing, I believe, to God’s total rejection of the first order of man. Samuel comes to it, “Jehovah has not chosen these”. The chosen one of Jehovah was not even invited to the conference. How sobering! but he was looking after the sheep. That was an expression of his heart. It sprang from love for Jehovah and for the sheep. I doubt not that Jehovah found him a man after His own heart because he loved the sheep. God refers elsewhere in a prophet to the sheep being men (see Ezekiel 34: 31). How carefully and wisely and lovingly David cared for the people of God.

Immediately he comes in the word is, “Arise, anoint him; for this is he”. We can always afford to wait for the Lord Jesus to come in. I believe He would come into all our occasions. Our motive and object should always be to anoint Him amongst us, this kind of Man. There is Himself personally in the circle where He is everything, but He also is in each one in character. I believe, dear brethren, the more we anoint Christ personally amongst us, the more scope the Holy Spirit has to form us in His character. Let us then come to God’s thoughts that the first has been terminated in the cross of Jesus and everything is established in Jesus risen.

I just refer to Peter, because here again he is in the presence of the “knower of the hearts of all”, and Jesus questions him. I think the Lord would question us like this, “Lovest thou me more than these?”. Naturally we have ambition and competition. Each one of us might suppose he loves the Lord Jesus above the others and therefore the Lord Jesus searches him.

Why is it recorded? Peter is with the Lord, and it is not just to tell us about the fact, but that we might come into the experience of being in the presence of the “knower of the hearts of all”. Jesus says to him the third time. You can understand Peter being grieved. First, do you love Me, Peter? and again, Do you love Me, Peter? Thirdly, Do you really love Me, Peter?—three times. I would be upset if someone asked me three times if I loved the Lord. But eventually Peter says, “Thou knowest all things”, ‘Thou knowest that I love Thee; Thou knowest I have been astray; Thou knowest I denied Thee; Thou knowest I have been impetuous and that I have failed; but Thou knowest that, underneath it all, I love Thee’. The Lord knew that, despite all, Peter really loved Him. So that the searching of the Lord Jesus but brings out in Peter the greater devotion, and it was the devotion of love.

So you see the link between love for Jesus and feeding His sheep. Judas had a commission without love for Christ. Peter had a commission and exercised it in love for Christ. Any service rendered to Him to be acceptable must spring from love for Him and His sheep. Peter had this. May the Lord grant that we may have it, that we may all by love serve one another, but by love. It was supremely seen in Jesus, but is to be seen in us as we give way to His Holy Spirit.

May the Lord help us all to contemplate the manhood of Jesus and, as giving place to His Spirit and giving place to the “knower of the hearts of all”, to be here more in His character for the Father’s pleasure. May He grant it for His name’s sake.

I thought that these passages would be an encouragement to us for we see in them the beginnings of the work of God in those apostles whom we have been considering in regard to their service. It is interesting how different their beginnings were, likewise how the sovereignty of the work of God came to light so as to bring persons into the activity which He intended to reveal to them. We also see the power of the Lord in resurrection; that He is above all, and that His operations can be hindered by no one. It says in the parable of the treasure in the field that the man bought the field. The Lord sold everything so as to buy this treasure and to possess the pearl. His rights are here seen in appropriating these persons, and also many others. Everything that God unfolds according to His will and purpose is founded on righteousness. He has the right to call you and me, and any other whom soever it may be.

It is His right, and the right of the Lord Jesus, who died to bring this scene under His domination. He says at the end of Matthew, “All power has been given me in heaven and upon earth”. We see power working in this world which might seem to our minds to be invincible, but it remains under His control. Nothing can be done and nothing can proceed without its being allowed by the Lord who is above all. He does according to His will, and the fruits of His activity come to light. In what way this may happen is His own prerogative.

We see this in these persons, and especially in Saul. How gladly we think of the example of his conversion! He was met by the Lord from the glory. The Lord of glory condescended to meet a man of whom we would say, ‘This is impossible—a most unlikely person to be the subject of such divine activity’. That shows what Jesus is; He is the Lord, and He works in His power in grace so as to produce something for the praise of the glory of God’s grace in vessels which are quite unworthy—and we are all that! None of us can attribute anything to ourselves that could have brought us near to God. It is pure grace and it was that, I believe, that had a continuing action with these persons right up to the end. The earliest transaction with the Lord is something that never leaves us. We see that in Paul. He shows us that his impression of this glorious light increased until finally he speaks of “a light above the brightness of the sun”, Acts 26: 13. That is a word we should notice, beloved, so as to arrive at something in ourselves. God’s calling is something wonderful. It is beyond our thoughts, beyond the realm of every human activity. Paul says in Galatians 1: 15, “God, who set me apart even from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace”. We sang in our hymn (No. 265) that God’s choice goes far back, even before the foundation of this world. Learned people calculate the age of the earth, and how old the creation—the stars and all else—may be, but what a lack there is of any apprehension of that which was even before that! They do not reach to those things. What is basic to divine working is hidden from the wise and prudent.

Let us consider what it means to us today, that we should be persons whom God has thought of before He created the visible things. Therein lies the great secret of our calling. We are called for a glory which reaches far beyond the time when everything physical no longer exists, for this earth and this visible heaven will pass away; but His word remains to eternity, and that which it brings to light as to ourselves is eternal. We can even today get a greater conception of that which is eternal. We are, as creatures, confined by temporal limitations, but we enjoy in the circle of the saints what God’s design for us is—eternal life and the enjoyment of it in His presence.

Thus these persons are introduced in a wonderful way. Is it not remarkable how activities in the locality of Damascus unfold in Acts 9? There are persons who are on the list to be brought to Jerusalem and there judged and probably put to death. So near had suffering and death come to these persons who were the objects of a work which Satan had instigated. But the Lord was there! He is Lord of all; the whole enmity of the wicked one must retreat when He appears, and the result is blessing. This man Saul is to be set free and secured so that Ananias comes to him and says, “Saul, brother, the Lord has sent me, Jesus that appeared to thee in the way in which thou camest, that thou mightest see, and be filled with the Holy Spirit”. What a wonderful word from a servant who had learned to be adjusted! He had raised objections, for he thought that things could not be so—‘We have heard what he has done in Jerusalem’. Now comes this change—it is the power of the Lord.

Now, the question for us is—Have we all had a real transaction with the Lord Jesus? Can we say anything about the One who has given Himself for us, and in His love has brought us near to Himself? And then comes the further question—To whom do I belong? There is to be the living evidence that we have heard His voice and that we are seeking the flock. Saul was brought to this flock. We cannot progress without local conditions and relationships with the brethren. Herein is seen the great thought that came into expression in the ministry of Paul—the body, and Christ as Head for ever.

When Paul at the close of his life writes to Timothy his view is directed to the appearing of the Lord and to the crown of righteousness which the Lord will render to him, then he says, “but not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing”, 2 Timothy 4: 8. Paul was not alone. He had been alone before Nero at his first defence, but he saw before God the great company with whom he was bound up and who even today are being gathered up to have part in this glory and to enter in where all is blessed and subsists before God in light and joy for eternity.
Referring briefly to the two apostles Peter and John, their beginning was likewise wonderful.

John was doubtless one of the two disciples mentioned in John 1: 35. He always kept himself in the background. That is a beautiful feature that makes room for what Christ is in His greatness. He is looking here on Jesus, and John the baptist says, “Behold the Lamb of God”. That was the basis for John’s leaving the Baptist. Was not the activity of John the baptist, and having to do with him, a blessed thing? Certainly. But there came a moment when Another put in His claim and established it, and John the evangelist yielded immediately. That word came, “Behold the Lamb of God”, and the two disciples heard him speaking and followed Jesus.

How the heart is moved when it is impressed with the greatness of Christ! Paul did not remain unmoved when he had seen the glory of the Lord—Oh, he pressed on; he did not stand still. He had an impression and because of this he moved on. Perhaps we have rather weak impressions of Christ and His greatness and therefore progress so little. But there can be increase, beloved. Let us get into His presence and the sight of His glory will bring transformation. So it is here. The Lord takes notice when someone follows Him. He turns round. Oh, He has a tender regard for the needs of a person who desires to follow Him, whose soul has been impressed with the call, “Behold the Lamb of God”. How much stands related to the Lord of glory! the “taking away of the sin of the world, in which your sins and mine are included, and the establishing of a world of blessing where sin can never again disturb. Sin is the separating element that has come in to keep us away from God’s thoughts and from His presence. But now He has come who has taken it upon Himself. Thus this movement of John’s disciples takes place, and the Lord takes notice of it. Now His question is, “What seek ye?”. It is now a question of what the soul longs for and where it desires to be. This is what we find with Paul also. What is your desire now that you are in relationship with Him? I believe we all confess the Lord Jesus as our Saviour; what is the next thing that your heart seeks and longs for?

They answer to His question by saying, “Rabbi (which being interpreted signifies Teacher), where abidest thou?”. This is a question which the Lord gladly answers—“Come and see”. Is this our desire—the presence of the Lord? Do we long to know Him in His own sphere?

We do not come to a company which has some kind of name or place on the earth; we come to Him. We may thus learn to know Him in His own sphere of activity, in His own abiding-place, which is surely the presence of the Father. We read earlier that they had seen something of His glory, “as of an only-begotten with a father”, the life that was seen here in Jesus. John even noticed the hour, it was about the tenth hour, and they remained that day with Him. There could be no going away. It says in Hebrews 10: 39, “But we are not drawers back”. God has no pleasure in such. How many have drawn back! Their impression of what they had seen and enjoyed was too weak. But in the presence of God, where Jesus appears, we think only of Him and His rights. The title Lamb of God involves His death and sufferings. The sacrificial thought goes right back to Adam’s sin when he fell. God Himself indeed took the knife in order to clothe that poor, sinful man. What is disclosed to us in the presence of the Lord is that He is supremely worthy that we should remain with Him. What instruction they must have received, for John says “and we have contemplated his glory, a glory as of an only-begotten with a father, full of grace and truth”, John 1: 14. What a wonderful thing to find the Lord in His own sphere! We experience it here today. The Lord comes to those who love Him and we can learn to know Him as we go on with this company in a committed way and when we truly value Him and that which is related to Him—the true path marked out by God.

Then there was Peter, who was also found. Andrew was a helper in this. His brotherly activity showed itself in this way, and the impression that Andrew had, aroused the interest of Peter. Andrew desired to interest Peter in what he had found. “We have found the Messias (which being interpreted is Christ)”. That is the great fulfilment of the promise that God had given to His people. The gain of all that God has promised is realised in the company which is heir to the divine assurance in the Person of Christ.

Now the Lord gives Peter a name; He says, “Thou art Simon, the son of Jonas; thou shalt be called Cephas”. The name Simon, son of Jonas, was his natural name, but now he receives a different name. He is called ‘stone’, which is connected with building. We find this also in other passages as, for example, Matthew 16: 18, where the Lord brings Peter in on the basis of his confession, “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God”.

The transactions which these men had in their original meeting with Christ left something permanent behind, and therefore I thought of the verses at the end of John where something of great importance is said. Peter is recovered in this chapter. The Lord did not leave this scene until things were fully in order. Let us remember what had happened and how the history of the disciples developed, particularly that of Peter. It is the same as many of us have found in ourselves. But the Lord is coming quickly and He would have us in every way prepared. John says, “Every one that has this hope in him purifies himself, even as he is pure”, 1 John 3: 3. We must be watchful as to everything that hinders our living in the presence of the Lord, so that we may be in liberty and always in the expectation of His coming. Thus did the Lord act before He left this scene. He cared for His disciples. He set them right as to what their failure had been, and He set them on ground where they were able to labour and work for Him. A great mission was implied in the name given to Peter.

Then comes John, and Peter wishes to raise a question; but we see that the Lord regulates the whole situation—“If I will that he abide until I come, what is that to thee?” Peter’s ministry is still available to us. That which was committed to him we must recognise and bow to and it regulates our course, though the public side is no longer to be seen. But there is something which remains and the Lord connects it with John and his ministry. Beloved, I believe we appreciate something of this at the present time, and as we bow and humble ourselves because of all the breakdown and the departure, we reach that which abides. They took this literally when they said, “That disciple does not die”. That was not the thought—the character of John’s ministry is what abides. When the Lord comes He will have something here which has continued according to His will and to which He will be attracted to come—and this is connected with what the apostle John has bequeathed to us. The admonitions which he gives us in view of eternal life have experienced no weakening. This glorious enjoyment which we are able to experience, and the links that bind us in true fellowship according to God’s thoughts, remain unchanged. All that is related to these blessings which John delineates is what keeps us in the last days on sure ground. May we be exercised therefore to continue on our way in close communion with the Lord, rejecting everything that man in his activities would bring in to hinder, and constantly maintaining self-judgment so as to be sensitive to what is pleasing to the Lord, so that at the end of our time we may be linked with what He had in mind in saying, “If I will that he abide until I come …”.

Well, beloved, we are at the close of this dispensation. We do not know how long there may be yet, but how do our hearts really stand in relation to Christ? How much have we received of that which radiates His glory, and of what the saints enjoy now who subject themselves to Him who directs all? May we be amongst these and rejoice in the ministry which gives us to know all that is given to us and which will abide, for His name’s sake.

I want to say a word about God’s ways with Job. It is a very interesting subject because it is one of the outstanding things in the Bible, I think, that God devotes forty-two chapters to speaking about His ways with one man. There must have been something very important in God’s ways with Job. He was no ordinary man; he was a remarkable man. God could say of him that there was none like him, outstanding in righteousness, outstanding in his piety, so much so that God could say to Satan, “Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth?”, Job 1: 8. Then Satan came back with a challenge and said, “Doth Job fear God for nought?”. He inferred that Job was serving God because it was profitable, because God was blessing him, and he says, in effect, ‘Take away the blessing and he will curse Thee’. Then Jehovah said to Satan, “All that he hath is in thy hand”; He allowed Satan to do what he would, with certain limitations. Satan immediately went to work to take away what God had given to Job. He smote his cattle, his sheep, his camels, he smote his sons; Job was bereft of all he had. A man who had been rich, a man God had blessed in a remarkable way, was reduced to poverty, yet he did not ascribe anything unseemly to God (Job 1: 22).

Then Satan said, “Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life”, Job 2: 4. He suggested that if Jehovah touched his body Job would curse Him. So God allowed Satan to touch Job in his body. He smote him with a great scourge. Job was covered with boils; yet he did not curse God. His wife told him to curse God and die, but he rebuked her—“Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. We have also received good from God, and should we not receive evil?”. Then it says that “In all this Job did not sin with his lips”. So Satan was defeated, and God could draw attention to Job, because He knew there was something more with him than what was external. What was external might not have stood the test, but there was something else. That is so with the saints; God’s work was there in Job.

So He could challenge Satan, and God was vindicated in His challenge that whatever Satan brought upon Job he could not get him to curse God. His links with God were stronger than what was merely material. It was proved he was not merely serving God because of the blessing God gave him. All those things were taken from him and he still did not curse God. That might have been the end of the matter; but God had in mind that He was going to get glory out of this; that was what He was working for. He had no interest in Satan, or in what Satan thought of His servant. Satan can only go so far; he can only do what God allows him to do, and what God allows him to do in divine wisdom is for God’s glory. This is a wonderful thing! That is what we see in this book.

Then three others come on the scene. I remember a brother calling them a ‘mutual irritation society’, because if there was anyone who would bring out anything that was in Job naturally, these men would. They did not understand God’s ways with Job, neither did they have any appreciation of Job, though they took the ground of being his friends. The things they said to Job provoked him bitterly. They brought out something in Job that had not come out before.

Job went to work to justify himself; he sought to show that he was just and even if it meant condemning God in His ways, which he did not understand, he was prepared to justify himself. So what these men brought out in Job was something which had not come out before; they brought out what he was as a natural man. They did not bring out the work of God; they brought out the flesh. And when it had all come out, when they had to give him up as a bad job, when Job appeared in so poor a light, when these men had done their worst and could do no more, then God brings another man on the scene who was different—a type of the Lord Jesus.

Elihu was a young man, but he went to work to get at the work of God in Job. He appeals to him, and brings out something from him. His service was so remarkable that when he brought it to a certain point. Jehovah came in in a whirlwind.

Jehovah brought Job to a point where he had to acknowledge that he had been talking about things of which he did not know anything; then he says, “I will lay my hand upon my mouth”. In effect, he said, I will just be quiet now because I do not know what I am talking about. But God says, No, that will not do; I am not satisfied with that. He says, “Gird up now thy loins like a man—I will demand of thee, and inform thou me”. Job had not been manly—many of us are like Job and are not manly with God. Now God says, “Gird up now thy loins like a man”. Face up to things, Job. What have you been saying about Me? Will it stand the test? Job had finally to come to it that not only had he been saying what he had not understood; not only had he been speaking about things that he did not know, but, above all, he had not really known God. He said, “I had heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee”. I do not think any man comes to a proper appreciation of the work of God in him, or of the flesh in him, until he knows God. Job had no idea of the depths of depravity that were connected with the flesh. Outwardly righteous, outwardly pious, yet deep inside there was the flesh. It had to come out. God allowed these three men to operate to bring out the flesh; and what capacity some men have to provoke and bring out the worst in men; but God can use these men, and use them to His end. He not only used Satan, but He used these three men; and it brought out the character of Job’s flesh, that he would even speak against God if it were a question of justifying himself. Because that was a sore point with Job—he prided himself in his righteousness; and outward righteousness there had been; there was no question as to that, no one could deny it; yet there was something lacking. But when all the flesh came out, when the worst came out in Job, then he said, “I had heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself and repent in dust and ashes”.

You may say, That righteous man, that man who has done so much that the fields could not complain against him, the furrows could not complain, his beasts could not complain, his neighbours could not complain; why is that same man now repenting in dust and ashes? Dust would connect itself with what man is, formed of the dust. It is very humbling to think of that, the first man was out of the earth, made of dust. Well, Job was recognising that he belonged to the first creation, that he was made of dust, and that would be very humbling.

And where you have ashes you have had fire. It would suggest that God had been working in His judgment, in His government; the fire had been there. It would speak of the death of Christ, the way the fire was there. Well, Job repents in dust and ashes. He recognises what he was natively, but he recognises that the fire had been there. Everything had been consumed; he cannot hold up his head, he has no reputation, he has nothing left in which he can boast. It has all been taken away by the fire.

So all that Job can speak about is, “But now mine eye seeth thee”. God came into his view and into his knowledge in a way He never had before, so much so that God could now say to these three men who had so provoked Job, “Ye have not spoken rightly of me, like my servant Job”. He spoke of dealing with them according to their folly and told them to take seven bullocks and seven rams as a burnt-offering, typically, to avail themselves of the death of Christ. The burnt-offering would speak of Christ as the ground of their acceptance, the bullocks speaking of the moral greatness of Christ as the burnt-offering. The rams would not be so large but would have their own distinctiveness, suggesting the progenitive idea, Christ as giving moral character to the whole flock. This would be the ground of their acceptance and would be effective, along with the prayer of Job.

Job would be in the gain of the burnt-offering now, for God says, “Him will I accept”. These men were told to bring these offerings and to “Go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt-offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you, for him will I accept; lest I deal with you after your folly, for ye have not spoken of me rightly, like my servant Job”.

Then it says they went and did according as Jehovah had said, and Jehovah accepted Job. There was something very wonderful that then came to light. It says, “And Jehovah turned the captivity of Job, when he had prayed for his friends”. It is a wonderful thing to have your captivity turned. It was not when Job spoke rightly of God, but when he prayed for his friends. This was the supreme test; it would really show whether Job had got down to the work of God in his soul, whether he had done with the flesh, and done with expecting anything from it, because it was these men who had so provoked him, so tested him, and so spoken of him. Now, can he pray for them? Can he operate in an intercessory way? If God is accepting Job now it is because he is standing typically in the gain of the work of Christ; he is standing in the gain of what he is according to God’s work. God is accepting him because he is now on that ground; he is not now on the ground of the flesh. He has vacated that; he is now standing on other ground and God has accepted him. Now the test is, is he great enough to be able to pray for his friends? He was. How interesting it would have been to hear him speaking to God for these men, beseeching God as he prayed for his friends.

Well, I have known what it is to have captivity turned. It is a wonderful thing! It means you have been in bondage and you are now in liberty. How wonderful it is!—the turning of the captivity. It is not only that you are freed, but you are brought into liberty, turned! God allows us to go into captivity in order that we might appreciate the liberty. Paul says, “Stand fast therefore, and be not held again in a yoke of bondage”, Galatians 5: 1. Well, Job came into liberty; he had never had liberty like it before. He had liberty with his brethren, and he had liberty with God, and the blessing of God came in. It says, “Jehovah blessed the latter end of Job”. He had twice as much as he had before—a wonderful thing that! Some of us are coming to what we might say was our latter end. Well, God blessed the latter end of Job. You might say, He blessed him as a young man. Well, he did bless him as a young man, but the blessing that came in in his old age was much greater as it was on a spiritual basis. His daughters were fairer, he had more cattle; and it all speaks of what is spiritual, of the way God would give us an appreciation of Himself and His things that we have not had before. That is a great blessing. So God blessed the latter end of Job.

James tells us, “Ye have heard of the endurance of Job”. Well, I would not have thought of that, but God says it. So Job had enough patience to go through this matter with God; he did not give up; and we want to have patience to go through. I am sure God is working with each one of us; He has an end in view, and it is a wonderful end; and what He has in view for us is that we should arrive at a judgment of the flesh, even the ‘best’, good as it might appear. We have to arrive at a judgment of it so that we say, “I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes”, as in the appreciation of what Christ is, and of the work of God, which is really Christ in the hearts of the saints. That is what God is bringing us to in a practical way. We all know this in the way of light; we can all quote from Romans, which tells us about the doctrine, but then have we arrived at it in an experimental way? That is what Job did; so you get the patience of Job and the end of the Lord. What a wonderful end it was! And James speaks of the Lord as being “full of tender compassion and pitiful”. You say, How do you work that out? Well, there it was; it did not appear on the surface; but how God felt for Job; His compassion was there in what Job was going through; His pity was there; but then God did not give up because He knew the end He was working to, and He knew what it was going to be for Job.

So as we pass through these things it is a good thing to remember that the Lord is of tender compassion and pitiful. God is never hard, never hard on His people. That was a terrible doctrine about God ambushing His people. That is not what I find here; there is tender compassion and pity and we all have to admit that it has been so. And if there is patience with us to get the gain of it, what a wonderful thing the end of the Lord is. It was good for Job, and God was glorified.

Well, let us all go through with God, let us not resist, let us put ourselves in the hands of God so that we may be brought to a knowledge of Himself. “Now mine eye seeth thee”; oh what a wonderful thing really to see God, really to know God! May the Lord bless the word, for His name’s sake.

TWO VIEWS OF A LONG LIFE—When Jacob was brought before Pharaoh by Joseph, Pharaoh enquired as to his age. Jacob’s reply was, “Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they do not attain to the days of the years of the life of my fathers”, Genesis 47: 9. Such feelings would find an echo in many a heart as we may have to recall sorrows and perhaps wasted time, periods when we may have been diverted from the happy path of obedience. That is one view. But in the next chapter, as Jacob blesses his grandsons, he says, “The God that shepherded me all my life long to this day, the Angel that redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads”. That is another view! Despite all that has happened we can look back and trace the way in which divine faithfulness has brought us through. The Holy Spirit, though grieved at times, has never left us, but has patiently pursued His gracious service, so that we might be brought into conformity with the great thoughts of divine purpose for us. So the Holy Spirit does not fail to give us His view of Jacob’s glorious departure; “By faith Jacob when dying blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshipped on the top of his staff”, Hebrews 11: 21.
Gone is the memory of the “few and evil” days; what is displayed is the final splendid result of the faithfulness of God—a worshipper!

‘ FIXED TIMES’—In Leviticus 23 we have the “set feasts of Jehovah”. A footnote in the New Translation gives the literal meaning of this as ‘Fixed times (for drawing near to God)’. What an attractive light this sheds upon our times of assembling. God marks them, and anticipates them with pleasure, and they should take priority in our arrangements. In relation to the passover, leading to the institution of the Lord’s supper, Luke 22: 14 says, “When the hour was come”. In Acts 3: 1 we have “the hour of prayer”, and in Luke 1: 10 “the hour of incense”. The Holy Spirit would help us to be ready in spiritual longings and alacrity for these ‘fixed times’, so that they may yield abundantly for divine pleasure, and then surely for our rich blessing. Individually, too, let us not fail to keep our ‘fixed times’ for drawing near to God.
